extracted.intended_audience: general readers and people interested in public relations / corporate communications (including PR practitioners, clients, and journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, practices and historical examples on how a global PR agency manages reputation, crisis communications, corporate/sectoral campaigns, training, and monitoring. Emphasis on crisis response, reputation framework, and ethical/strategic tactics used by an agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation capital framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and actively manage 'reputation capital' across four areas: company actions, communications, social narratives, and stakeholder beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burson uses a framework and consulting methodology to assess and actively manage reputation capital across these four areas; this functions as an organizing rubric for client work (strategy should address each area).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communication target audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: During crises, provide communication with clients' employees, customers and the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Services include communications directed at internal (employees), customer-facing, and mass/public audiences; the Issues & Crisis Group explicitly lists these target groups as recipients of crisis messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency and crisis planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Assist clients in developing contingency plans for potential crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond reactive work, the firm provides planning and preparedness services so clients have pre-established responses and protocols for likely crisis scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence reports and monitoring cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide intelligence reports to clients hourly or daily advising of new issues, public reception, and critical or supportive responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring frequency (hourly/daily) and structured intelligence updates are part of crisis practice; guidance implies rapid, regular situational awareness to inform communications and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based / data-driven communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'DIGS' (digital, integrated, global, strategic) and 'Evidence-Based Communications' — a scientific and data-driven approach to communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced by leadership (Mark Penn) as a strategic approach; implies using research, polling, and data to shape messaging and measure impact rather than relying solely on intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training for consistency and cultural appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide comprehensive employee training to create a uniform approach to public relations worldwide while remaining culturally appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burson-Marsteller University and ongoing training aimed to make communications consistent across clients and locations but adapted to cultural contexts; includes specific training for crisis teams to 'communicate the correct information' during crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mass media and large-scale publicity events
rubrics_metrics.description: Execute televised press conferences and large-scale publicity events to reach broad audiences and generate visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tylenol press conference televised across 35 markets; organizing events like the AT&T Olympic Torch Relay and Hands Across America; appropriate channel selection and event scale are used as tools in major campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology, humility, and public contrition as strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise clients to 'be humble' and apologize when appropriate to restore public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Burson advised Coca‑Cola to be humble and apologize during the New Coke episode; guidance implies that timely contrition can be a central element of restoring reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend corrective product/business actions and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend tangible corrective actions (recalls, product redesigns, safety measures) alongside transparent communication to rebuild trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Johnson & Johnson/Tylenol — nationwide recall, televised briefings, introduction of tamper‑proof packaging and replacement offers; PR counsel combined messaging with concrete corporate actions to demonstrate responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized certified crisis teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a global crisis practice with specially certified experts dedicated to crisis management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Issues & Crisis Group had a network of specially certified experts; implies using specialized, credentialed teams rather than ad-hoc staffing for high-stakes incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and ethical disclosure (avoid undisclosed influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose client relationships and avoid tactics that create the appearance of grassroots support or undisclosed paid influence (astroturfing/whisper campaigns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern examples: organizing front groups (National Smokers Alliance) and undisclosed 'whisper campaigns' or pitching articles without revealing client ties (Facebook/Google incident) — these tactics generated criticism and backfired; guidance implies ethical disclosure is a criterion for acceptable practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client selection and reputational risk assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider long-term reputational consequences of client engagements and be prepared for public criticism tied to controversial clients or industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burson faced criticism for work with tobacco, authoritarian regimes, and controversial governments; the firm later committed (2010) to no longer accept tobacco work, illustrating client selection as a reputational criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector- and audience-specific communications practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor communications by sector (e.g., corporate, healthcare, technology, public affairs) and by sub-specialty (corporate brand positioning, financial communications, C‑suite positioning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The firm organized practices by sector (healthcare, technology, corporate, public affairs) and developed specialized campaigns (e.g., National Breast Cancer Awareness Month), indicating that effective messaging must be customized to sector norms, regulations, and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-crisis recovery communications and reputation rebuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide communications tools and techniques intended to help companies recover following a crisis, including market research into CEO and corporate reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Services include research-driven recovery programs, ongoing reputation measurement (e.g., time to recover reputation), and messaging strategies aimed at restoring confidence over months/years; Burson's research noted reputation recovery timelines (e.g., 3.2 years reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of third-party spokespeople and earned media tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage former journalists, spokespeople, and third-party voices to push narratives and secure earned media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include hiring former reporters to promote critical coverage (Google 'whisper campaign') and setting up interviews/press placements for client representatives to influence coverage; guidance implies careful use of third-party voices but also warns of disclosure/ethical risks.
